articles.headline: Meet the 'jungle penguin' with yellow eyebrows
articles.standfirst: In New Zealand, volunteers are learning the secrets of a shy penguin that lives in the forest.
body: In the south of New Zealand there is a big national park called Fiordland. It has deep, cold water, high mountains and a thick rainforest. A very special penguin lives there: the tawaki, or Fiordland crested penguin. It is about half a metre tall and it has bright yellow 'eyebrows'.

Most penguins live together in big groups on beaches or on ice. But the tawaki is different. It makes its nest alone, in a hole under the trees of the forest. That is why one scientist calls it a 'jungle penguin'.

A team of volunteers called the Tawaki Project started to study these birds in 2014. This September, they found 93 nests on two islands. In 12 years they have found 1,200 nests. The scientists say there are about three times more tawaki than people thought before. But they want to learn more, because the number of these penguins is going down.

the place where a bird lays its eggs and keeps its babies

articles.headline: Looking for a lost plane on a faraway island
articles.standfirst: Researchers have travelled to a small Pacific island to try to solve the mystery of Amelia Earhart.
body: Amelia Earhart was a famous American pilot. In 1937 she tried to fly around the world with her navigator, Fred Noonan. But their plane disappeared over the Pacific Ocean, and nobody found them. It is still one of the big mysteries of history.

Now a team of researchers from the United States has travelled to Nikumaroro, a small island in the Pacific. It is part of the country of Kiribati. Their ship sailed for five days to get there. In 2020, a satellite photo showed a strange object in the water near the island. Some people think it is part of Earhart's plane. Others think it is only an old tree.

The team wants to look at the object carefully. But it is not easy. The weather can be bad, and there are giant coconut crabs on the island. They come out at night, so the researchers sleep on their ship.

articles.headline: Welcome home: 342 treasures return to Peru
articles.standfirst: A painting, a hand-written book and hundreds of other objects have come back from six countries.
body: Peru has received 342 objects that are part of its cultural heritage. For years, these pieces of art and history were in other countries. Now they are back home. On Wednesday 7 October, at Torre Tagle Palace in Lima, the Foreign Affairs Minister, Carlos Espa, handed them over to the Culture Minister, Alberto Beingolea.

The objects came back from six countries: Germany, Argentina, Belgium, Brazil, the United States and the United Kingdom. Peru's embassies worked together with police forces and other organisations in those countries to find them. Some people abroad also decided to give pieces back on their own. It was the largest return of cultural objects to Peru so far this year. Minister Espa thanked everyone who helped and said that protecting Peru's heritage is a priority for his ministry.

Among the treasures there is a large painting called 'The Transit of St. Joseph', which is very important for its history and its art. There is also a special book written by hand, 'Ancient Peruvian Art', with beautiful watercolour pictures.

The Culture Minister explained that the work is not finished. His team also watches social media, because people often offer these objects for sale online. Soon, everyone will be able to see the returned pieces at a special exhibition in the Culture Ministry.

a kind of paint that you mix with water
a show of art or objects that people can visit and look at

articles.headline: Never give up: a surprise winner in Shanghai
articles.standfirst: Spain's Alejandro Davidovich Fokina came back from a set down to beat the top seed, Alexander Zverev.
body: Spanish tennis player Alejandro Davidovich Fokina has reached the final of the Shanghai Masters in China after a surprising win. On Saturday he beat Alexander Zverev from Germany, who was the top seed – the player the organisers expected to do best in the tournament. The score was 5-7, 6-4, 6-3.

Zverev won the first set, and for a while it looked like an easy day for him. But Davidovich Fokina did not give up. He won the second set after an amazing backhand shot that he hit while he was running, and the crowd stood up to cheer. In the third set he started strongly, went 2-0 up and never lost control of the match. The game lasted just over two hours.

It was only his second win against Zverev in eight matches. After the game, he said he felt stronger physically in the third set, and that he tried to enjoy playing instead of thinking about the result. Zverev, who is 29, said he was tired and had a small injury, and that he needed a break.

Davidovich Fokina has now won nine matches in a row in China. Last month he won a tournament in the city of Chengdu. In the final on Sunday he will play Daniil Medvedev or another Spanish player, Rafael Jodar.

a player who the organisers think is one of the best in a competition

articles.headline: The books that moved the Earth go on sale
articles.standfirst: First editions by Copernicus, Galileo and Newton are on show in New York before an auction that could raise US$7 million.
body: A. Some of the most important books in the history of science are on display in New York this month – and anyone with a few million dollars to spare could soon take them home. Hundreds of rare volumes are being shown at the auction house Sotheby's before they are sold on Tuesday, 20 October.

B. The highlights are works by three men who transformed our picture of the universe between 1543 and 1687: Nicolaus Copernicus, Galileo Galilei and Isaac Newton. Copernicus argued that the Earth moves around the Sun, Galileo used his telescope to support that view, and Newton explained the laws of gravity that keep the planets in their orbits. Together, their ideas challenged what the Roman Catholic Church taught at the time.

C. According to Sotheby's, many of the books have spent decades in private collections and are only now coming back onto the market. The Copernicus volume has the highest estimate: it could sell for up to US$1 million. Altogether, the auction house expects the sale to raise as much as US$7 million.

D. Surprisingly, visitors are allowed to handle the books. Gloves are not necessary, as long as people wash their hands carefully first. Richard Austin, who leads Sotheby's books and manuscripts department worldwide, says looking at the pages online is one thing, but holding a book that changed our understanding of the universe is 'a very different experience'.

E. Not everyone is happy when such treasures disappear into private homes, where researchers and the public may never see them again. However, Nick Wilding, a historian of science at Georgia State University, believes that rare books usually find their way to public institutions in the end – partly because universities and libraries tend to outlive individual collectors.

glossary.d: a sale where things are sold to the person who offers the most money
books, especially old or important ones
a guess about the value or size of something

to live or exist longer than someone or something else

articles.headline: Too many bees? Honeybees push wild insects off flowers
articles.standfirst: A two-year study in England found that honeybees often win the fight for pollen and nectar – sometimes by force.
body: Bees are often seen as heroes of the natural world, and campaigns to 'save the bees' have inspired thousands of people in the UK to take up beekeeping as a hobby. The number of registered beekeepers more than doubled between 2010 and 2025, from 19,000 to 47,000. But a new study suggests that all these extra honeybees may be causing problems for other insects. Experts were already concerned that large numbers of hives could spread diseases to wild bees and leave less food for them, especially in places with few flowers.

Researchers from Anglia Ruskin University spent two years watching pollinators feed on bramble and ivy flowers near honeybee hives in Cambridgeshire. They recorded 300 encounters between honeybees, bumblebees, solitary bees, hoverflies and other insects, noting each time which one 'won' access to the flower, which one 'lost', or whether they shared it.

Honeybees won most of the contests, and where there were more honeybees, there were fewer wild pollinators. Scientists already knew that honeybees could compete indirectly, simply by taking pollen and nectar before others arrived. What the study revealed was direct aggression: in about a fifth of the contests that honeybees won, they landed on rivals, pushed them off flowers or chased them away. Bumblebees sometimes knocked other insects off too, but the lead author, Victoria Buckle, believes this was usually an accident caused by their clumsy flying. She thinks the honeybees' behaviour may be linked to the way their colonies are organised, since some honeybees act as guards that defend the hive.

Only one species stood up to the honeybees: the ivy bee, which was first recorded in the UK in 2001. The study also found that contests became more frequent on hotter days, probably because flowers produce less nectar in the heat. With summers expected to get warmer, the researchers think this kind of competition may become more common.

articles.headline: The insect that never was: AI fakes put citizen science on guard
articles.standfirst: A convincing photo of an unknown mantis turned out to be machine-made – one sign of a wider flood of 'AI slop' in science.
body: For a few seconds, Kris Anderson thought he had found something extraordinary. The photograph showed a dead-leaf mantis, an insect whose flat, brown, crinkled body imitates the leaves on a forest floor – but this one's camouflage was so perfect that it seemed to be wearing a real leaf. Anderson, who keeps thousands of preserved specimens at his home in Las Vegas, had never seen anything like it. Then the truth dawned on him: the creature had never existed. It was a fake, produced by artificial intelligence.

Anderson is not a professional scientist. After his day job as director of a counselling centre, he spends two and a half hours every evening checking the 500 or 600 mantis photographs that members of the public upload to iNaturalist, a website where anyone can record wildlife sightings to help map the planet's biodiversity. Most images are unremarkable, but occasionally one is genuinely valuable – the first record of a species on the Caribbean island of Aruba, for example.

His experience on 17 June, reported this week by The New York Times, is one small example of a much wider problem. The same algorithms that make some research tasks easier are flooding science with low-quality, machine-made material, often called 'AI slop'. Academic journals are receiving papers padded with references to articles that do not exist, and some reviewers who are supposed to catch such errors are quietly handing the job to AI themselves.

Ironically, some of the projects hit hardest are those designed to open science up to everyone, and they are now having to build defences. The online archive arXiv, which publishes research quickly with less checking than traditional journals, has begun limiting submissions. eBird, Cornell University's database of bird sightings, introduced a warning system in August to flag artificial or heavily edited images, and iNaturalist is considering similar measures. Last spring OpenStreetMap, a map of the world built by volunteers, even added a special 'read me' file aimed at the automated programs that edit its shared code. Whether volunteers like Anderson can keep up remains an open question.

articles.headline: From hyperinflation to the region's lowest: how Peru tamed rising prices
articles.standfirst: At the IMF and World Bank meetings in Bangkok, the head of Peru's central bank explained the reforms behind a remarkable record.
body: When officials meet to share stories about economic reforms that worked, Peru now has one worth telling. This week in Bangkok, at the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank, the governor of Peru's Central Reserve Bank (BCR), Julio Velarde, joined officials from Portugal, Papua New Guinea and Rwanda on a panel about success stories, chaired by the IMF's deputy managing director, Nigel Clarke. His central claim was striking: so far this century, Peru has had the lowest inflation in Latin America.

That achievement looks all the more remarkable given where the country started. In the late 1980s, Peru suffered hyperinflation, when prices rose so quickly that money lost its value almost overnight. Velarde explained that today's system was built in response to that crisis. A key pillar is the bank's independence, written into law in 1992, which forbids it from lending to the government or to state development banks, and from setting several exchange rates at once. Peru was also the first country in Latin America to let its currency float freely, which made it easier to absorb sudden shocks, and in 2001 the bank adopted an explicit inflation target.

Another legacy of hyperinflation was 'dollarisation': because Peruvians had lost faith in their own currency, many prices and loans were in US dollars. Reversing this, Velarde said, required more than keeping inflation as low as in the United States. Prices also had to be quoted in soles, and banks were required to hold extra reserves when they lent in dollars. As a result, the share of loans in dollars fell from 81% in 2000 to 23% today.

The framework has since been tested by periods of great uncertainty, such as the 2008 global financial crisis and the COVID-19 pandemic. According to Velarde, having the right tools and the flexibility to use them made the difference. He even pointed out that Peru's core inflation this century has been lower than that of the United States – a claim that would have sounded unbelievable in the late 1980s.
